title: Dating Needs a Destination 2026
author: Daniel Cox
source: Institute for Family Studies (ifstudies.org), excerpt from Generation Uncoupled, October 30,
summary: In this excerpt from his book Generation Uncoupled, Daniel Cox argues that modern dating feels directionless because Americans no longer agree on its purpose. Where courtship once moved from meeting to dating to relationship to marriage and children, declining interest in marriage and parenthood among teenagers, especially girls, has removed the shared destination that gave dating its parameters. As norms widen to accept polyamory and open arrangements, flexibility is prized over permanence, and young singles are left in 'relationship purgatory' with partners who exploit the ambiguity. Cox cites research that close to four in ten young adults have been in an undefined relationship and that married people report markedly higher trust than cohabiters. His conclusion is that ambiguity feels safer than commitment but erodes confidence in our partner and ourselves, whereas marriage, as a future-oriented institution, forces couples to think about what lies ahead.
points: Dating once had a shared destination of marriage and family; as that purpose weakens, the whole process loses its signposts.
Teen girls' interest in marriage fell from 83 percent in 1993 to 61 percent in 2023, and fewer than half of teens now think parenthood is at least fairly likely.
When relationships exist chiefly to serve personal interests, flexibility beats permanence and ambiguity favors whoever wants less commitment.
Close to four in ten young adults report an undefined relationship, which produces anxiety and a sense of being lost.
Marriage generates more trust than cohabitation, and its future orientation is what ambiguity cannot supply.
quotes: The purpose of dating was to find a single person with whom to build a family. However imperfectly a couple might come together, the relational goals of marriage and family formation helped establish clear parameters.
If the purpose of dating is less clear than it once was, it’s because marriage and parenthood are less desirable goals for many young people today.

If relationships are evolving to primarily function to serve our personal interests, it makes sense that any configuration might be a plausible option. Flexibility is prioritized over permanence, mutual betterment, or stability.
More young singles are left in a kind of relationship purgatory with partners who take full advantage of the ambiguity with little social pressure to clarify their interests or intent.
We found that close to four in ten young adults reported having ever been in a romantic or sexual relationship that was undefined, which means they were uncertain how to describe the relationship.
An ambiguous relationship status can sometimes feel safer than fully committing, but it undermines the confidence we have in our partner and ourselves. It keeps us locked in the present.
Marriage is a uniquely future-oriented institution; it compels us to think about what lies ahead.
